entries.0e11247e8ae290f84bf563410cfcac6c79fe344e: <div sID="gen20935" type="x-p"/> <chapter n="10" osisID="Zech.10" sID="Zech.10"/> <div eID="gen20935" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20936" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen20937" type="x-p"/> The scope of this chapter is much the same with that of the foregoing chapter—to encourage the Jews that had returned with hopes that though they had been under divine rebukes for their negligence in rebuilding the temple, and were now surrounded with enemies and dangers, yet God would do them good, and make them prosperous at home and victorious abroad. Now, I. They are here directed to eye the great God in all events that concerned them, and, both in the evils they suffered and in the comforts they desired, to acknowledge his hand, <reference osisRef="Zech.10.1-Zech.10.4">ver. 1-4</reference>. II. They are encouraged to expect strength and success from him in all their struggles with the enemies of their church and state, and to hope that the issue would be glorious at last, <reference osisRef="Zech.10.5-Zech.10.12">ver. 5-12</reference>.
entries.66e139d1481333e6937b29121bc97a1da38e9a42: <div eID="gen20937" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen20936" type="introduction"/> <title type="x-s3">Encouragements to Trust in God. (<hi type="small-caps">b. c.</hi> 510.)</title> <div sID="gen20938" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">1</hi> Ask ye of the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> rain in the time of the latter rain; <hi type="italic">so</hi> the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> shall make bright clouds, and give them showers of rain, to every one grass in the field. <hi type="super">2</hi> For the idols have spoken vanity, and the diviners have seen a lie, and have told false dreams; they comfort in vain: therefore they went their way as a flock, they were troubled, because <hi type="italic">there was</hi> no shepherd. <hi type="super">3</hi> Mine anger was kindled against the shepherds, and I punished the goats: for the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> of hosts hath visited his flock the house of Judah, and hath made them as his goodly horse in the battle. <hi type="super">4</hi> Out of him came forth the corner, out of him the nail, out of him the battle bow, out of him every oppressor together. <div eID="gen20938" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20939" type="x-p"/> Gracious things and glorious ones, very glorious and very gracious, were promised to this poor afflicted people in the foregoing chapter; now here God intimates to them that he will <hi type="italic">for these things be enquired of</hi> by them, and that he expects they should acknowledge him in all their ways and in all his ways towards them—and not idols that were rivals with him for their respects. <div eID="gen20939" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20940" type="x-p"/> I. The prophet directs them to apply to God by prayer for rain in the season thereof. He had promised, in the close of the foregoing chapter, that there should be great plenty of corn and wine, whereas for several years, by reason of unseasonable weather, there had been great scarcity of both; but the earth will not yield its fruits unless the heavens water it, and therefore they must look up to God for the <hi type="italic">dew of heaven,</hi> in order to the fatness and fruitfulness of the earth (<reference osisRef="Zech.10.1">v. 1</reference>): "<hi type="italic">Ask you of the Lord rain.</hi> Do not pray to the clouds, nor to the stars, for rain, but <hi type="italic">to the Lord;</hi> for he it is that <hi type="italic">hears the heavens,</hi> when they <hi type="italic">hear the earth,</hi>" <reference osisRef="Hos.2.21">Hos. ii. 21</reference>. Seasonable rain is a great mercy, which we must <hi type="italic">ask of God, rain in the time of the latter rain,</hi> when there is most need of it. The former rain fell at the seed-time, in autumn, the latter fell in the spring, between March and May, which brought the corn to an ear and filled it. If either of these rains failed, it was very bad with that land; for from the end of May to September they never had any rain at all. Jerome, who lived in Judea, says that he never saw any rain there in June or July. They are directed to ask for it <hi type="italic">in the time</hi> when it used to come. Note, We must, in our prayers, dutifully attend the course of Providence; we must ask for mercies in their proper time, and not expect that God should go out of his usual way and method for us. But, since sometimes God denied rain in the usual time as a token of his displeasure, they must pray for it then as a token of his favour, and they shall not pray in vain. <hi type="italic">Ask and it shall be given you. So the Lord shall make bright clouds</hi> (which, though they are without rain themselves, are yet presages of rain)—<hi type="italic">lightnings</hi> (so the margin reads it), for <hi type="italic">he maketh lightnings for the rain.</hi> He will <hi type="italic">give them showers of rain</hi> in great abundance, and so give to <hi type="italic">every one grass in the field;</hi> for God is universally good, and <hi type="italic">makes his rain to fall upon the just and the unjust.</hi> <div eID="gen20940" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20941" type="x-p"/> II. He shows them the folly of making their addresses to idols as their fathers had done (<reference osisRef="Zech.10.2">v. 2</reference>): <hi type="italic">The idols have spoken vanity;</hi> the teraphim, which they courted and consulted in their distress, were so far from being able to command rain for them that they could not so much as tell them when they should have rain. They pretended to promise them rain at such a time, but it did not come. <hi type="italic">The diviners,</hi> who were the prophets of those idols, <hi type="italic">have seen a lie</hi> (their visions were all a cheat and a sham); and <hi type="italic">they have told false dreams,</hi> such as the event did not answer, which proved that they were not from God. Thus they <hi type="italic">comforted in vain</hi> those that consulted the lying oracles; all the <hi type="italic">vanities of the heathen</hi> put together could not <hi type="italic">give rain,</hi> <reference osisRef="Jer.14.22">Jer. xiv. 22</reference>. Yet this was not the worst of it; they not only got nothing by the false gods, but they lost the favour of the true God, for <hi type="italic">therefore they went their way</hi> into captivity <hi type="italic">as a flock</hi> driven into the fold, and <hi type="italic">they were troubled</hi> with one vexation after another, as scattered sheep are, <hi type="italic">because there was no shepherd,</hi> no prince to rule them, no priest to intercede for them, none to take care of them and keep them together. Those that wandered after strange gods were made to wander, into strange nations. <div eID="gen20941" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20942" type="x-p"/> III. He shows them the hand of God in all the events that concerned them, both those that made against them and those that made for them, <reference osisRef="Zech.10.3">v. 3</reference>. Let them consider, 1. When every thing went cross it was God that walked contrary to them (<reference osisRef="Zech.10.3">v. 3</reference>): "<hi type="italic">My anger was kindled against the shepherds</hi> that should have fed the flock, but neglected it, and starved it. I was displeased at the wicked magistrates and ministers, the idol-shepherds." The captivity in Babylon was a token of God's anger against them; in it likewise he <hi type="italic">punished the goats,</hi> those of the flock that were filthy and mischievous; they were set on the left hand, to go away into punishment. Though the body of the nation suffered in the captivity, yet it was only the goats and the shepherds that God was angry with, and that he punished; the same affliction to others came from the love of God, and was but a fatherly chastisement, which to them came from his wrath, and was a judicial punishment. 2. When things began to change for the better it was God that gave them the happy turn. "He has now <hi type="italic">visited his flock</hi> with favour, to enquire after them, and provides what he finds proper for them, and he has made them <hi type="italic">as his goodly horse in the battle,</hi> has beautified them, taken care of them, managed and made use of them, as a man does the horse he rides on, has made them valuable in themselves and formidable to those about them, <hi type="italic">as his goodly horse.</hi>" It is God that makes us what we are, and it is with us as he appoints. <div eID="gen20942" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20943" type="x-p"/> IV. He shows them that every creature is to them what God makes it to be (<reference osisRef="Zech.10.4">v. 4</reference>): <hi type="italic">Out of him came forth the corner, out of him the nails.</hi> 1. All the power that was engaged against them was from God. <hi type="italic">Out of him</hi> came all the combined force of their enemies; every <hi type="italic">oppressor together</hi> (and the oppressors of Israel were not a few) did but what his hand and his counsel determined before to be done; nor could they have had such power against them unless it had been given them from above. 2. All the power likewise that was engaged for them was derived from him and depended on him. Out of him came forth <hi type="italic">the corner-stone</hi> of the building, the power of magistrates, which keeps the several parts of the state together. Princes are often called the <hi type="italic">corners of the people,</hi> as <reference osisRef="1Sam.14.38">1 Sam. xiv. 38</reference>, marg. Out of him came forth <hi type="italic">the nail</hi> that fixed the state, the <hi type="italic">nail in the sure place</hi> (<reference osisRef="Isa.22.23">Isa. xxii. 23</reference>), the <hi type="italic">nail in his holy place,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ezra.9.8">Ezra ix. 8</reference>. Out of him came forth <hi type="italic">the battle-bow,</hi> the military power, and out of him <hi type="italic">every oppressor,</hi> or exactor, that had the civil power in his hand; and therefore to God, the fountain of power, we must always have an eye, and see every man's judgment proceeding from him.
entries.8480d32326bc28446f8434df43e1bc9aa6fcd293: <div eID="gen20943" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">Evangelical Promises; Encouraging Prospects. (<hi type="small-caps">b. c.</hi> 510.)</title> <div sID="gen20944" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">5</hi> And they shall be as mighty <hi type="italic">men,</hi> which tread down <hi type="italic">their enemies</hi> in the mire of the streets in the battle: and they shall fight, because the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> <hi type="italic">is</hi> with them, and the riders on horses shall be confounded. <hi type="super">6</hi> And I will strengthen the house of Judah, and I will save the house of Joseph, and I will bring them again to place them; for I have mercy upon them: and they shall be as though I had not cast them off: for I <hi type="italic">am</hi> the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> their God, and will hear them. <hi type="super">7</hi> And <hi type="italic">they of</hi> Ephraim shall be like a mighty <hi type="italic">man,</hi> and their heart shall rejoice as through wine: yea, their children shall see <hi type="italic">it,</hi> and be glad; their heart shall rejoice in the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> . <hi type="super">8</hi> I will hiss for them, and gather them; for I have redeemed them: and they shall increase as they have increased. <hi type="super">9</hi> And I will sow them among the people: and they shall remember me in far countries; and they shall live with their children, and turn again. <hi type="super">10</hi> I will bring them again also out of the land of Egypt, and gather them out of Assyria; and I will bring them into the land of Gilead and Lebanon; and <hi type="italic">place</hi> shall not be found for them. <hi type="super">11</hi> And he shall pass through the sea with affliction, and shall smite the waves in the sea, and all the deeps of the river shall dry up: and the pride of Assyria shall be brought down, and the sceptre of Egypt shall depart away. <hi type="super">12</hi> And I will strengthen them in the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> ; and they shall walk up and down in his name, saith the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> . <div eID="gen20944" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20945" type="x-p"/> Here are divers precious promises made to the people of God, which look further than to the state of the Jews in the latter days of their church, and have certain reference to the spiritual Israel of God, the gospel-church, and all true believers. <div eID="gen20945" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20946" type="x-p"/> I. They shall have God's favour and presence, and shall be owned and accepted of him. This is the foundation of all the rest: <hi type="italic">The Lord is with them,</hi> <reference osisRef="Zech.10.5">v. 5</reference>. He espouses their cause, takes their part, is on their side; and, if he be for them, who can be against them? Again (<reference osisRef="Zech.10.6">v. 6</reference>), <hi type="italic">I have mercy upon them.</hi> All their dignity and joy are owing purely to God's mercy; and mercy, as it supposes misery, so it excludes merit. They had been cast off, the effect of which could not but be misery; they had been justly cast off, and therefore could pretend to merit nothing at God's hand but wrath and the curse; yet it is promised, <hi type="italic">They shall be as though I had not cast them off.</hi> The transgressions of their fathers, for which they had been rejected, shall not only not be visited upon them, but shall not be so much as remembered against them. God will be as perfectly reconciled to them as if he had never contended with them, and the falling out of these lovers shall rather be the renewing than the weakening of love. They shall have such a full assurance of God's being reconciled to them, and upon that shall be so well reconciled to themselves, that they shall be as easy as if they had never been cast off; and their condition, after their restoration to the divine favour, shall be so very happy that there shall not remain the least scar from the wounds which were given them by their being cast off. Such favour does God show to returning repenting sinners, who were by nature at a distance, and children of wrath; such fellowship are they admitted into, and such freedom does he use with them, that they are <hi type="italic">as though they had never been cast off.</hi> 1. The covenant they are admitted into is the same that ever it was: <hi type="italic">I am the Lord their God,</hi> according to the original contract, the covenant made with their fathers. 2. The communion they are admitted into is the same that ever it was: <hi type="italic">I will hear them.</hi> They shall be as welcome as ever to speak to him, and as sure as ever to receive from him an answer of peace; for, as he never did, so he never will, say to Jacob's seed, <hi type="italic">Seek you me in vain.</hi> <div eID="gen20946" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20947" type="x-p"/> II. They shall be victorious over their enemies, that would draw them from either their duty to God or their comfort in God (<reference osisRef="Zech.10.5">v. 5</reference>): <hi type="italic">They shall be as mighty men,</hi> that are both strong in body and bold in spirit, men of vigour, men of valour, effective men. <hi type="italic">Those of Ephraim,</hi> as well as those of Judah, shall be <hi type="italic">like a mighty man</hi> (<reference osisRef="Zech.10.7">v. 7</reference>), that dares to go about a difficult enterprise and is able to go through with it. They shall, as mighty men, <hi type="italic">tread down their enemies in the battle,</hi> as the dirt that is thrown out of the houses is trodden with other dirt <hi type="italic">in the mire of the streets.</hi> And <hi type="italic">they shall</hi> therefore <hi type="italic">fight, because the Lord is with them.</hi> Some would argue that they may <hi type="italic">therefore</hi> sit still, and do nothing, because the Lord is with them, who can and will do all. No; God's gracious presence with us to help us must not supersede, but quicken and animate, our endeavours to help ourselves; and we must therefore <hi type="italic">work out our salvation with fear and trembling,</hi> because <hi type="italic">it is God that works in us both to will and to do.</hi> They shall fight with readiness and resolution because, if God be with them, they are sure to be conquerors, more than conquerors. For then <hi type="italic">the riders on horses shall be confounded.</hi> The cavalry of the enemies shall be routed, and put into disorder, by the infantry of the Jews. The preachers of the gospel of Christ went forth to war a good warfare; they charged bravely, because God was with them; and the <hi type="italic">riders on horses</hi> that opposed them <hi type="italic">were confounded,</hi> for God chose the <hi type="italic">weak</hi> and <hi type="italic">foolish things of the world to confound the wise and mighty.</hi> But whence have they all this might? How come they to be so able, so active? It is in the Lord, and in the power of his might, that they are so (<reference osisRef="Zech.10.6">v. 6</reference>): <hi type="italic">I will strengthen the house of Judah,</hi> and <hi type="italic">so I will save the house of Joseph.</hi> Note, God saves us by strengthening us, and works out our happiness by working in us to do our duty. And thus we are engaged to the utmost diligence in using the strength God gives us; and yet, when all is done, God must have the glory of all. God is our strength, and so becomes both our song and our salvation. <div eID="gen20947" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20948" type="x-p"/> III. Those of them that are dispersed shall be gathered together into one body (<reference osisRef="Zech.10.6">v. 6</reference>): <hi type="italic">I will bring them again to place them,</hi> bring them from other lands to place them in their own land. This was a token of their being perfectly restored to all their other ancient privileges—they shall be restored to the possession of their own land. This was fulfilled when the <hi type="italic">children of God that were scattered abroad</hi> were by faith in Christ incorporated in the gospel-church, and Jews and Gentiles became <hi type="italic">one fold,</hi> <reference osisRef="John.10.16">John x. 16</reference>. In order to this (<reference osisRef="Zech.10.8">v. 8</reference>) <hi type="italic">I will hiss for them,</hi> or, rather, <hi type="italic">whistle</hi> for them, as the shepherd with his pipe calls his sheep together, that <hi type="italic">know his voice;</hi> and so <hi type="italic">I will gather them.</hi> The preaching of the gospel was, as it were, God's hissing for souls to come to Jesus Christ, his calling in his scattered sheep to the green pastures. <hi type="italic">I will gather them, for I have redeemed them.</hi> Note, Those whom Christ has redeemed by his blood God will gather by his grace, as a <hi type="italic">hen gathers her brood under her wings.</hi> This promise is enlarged upon <reference osisRef="Zech.10.10">v. 10</reference>, <hi type="italic">I will bring them again also out of the land of Egypt.</hi> Some think this was literally fulfilled when Ptolemæus Philadelphus king of Egypt sent 120,000 Jews out of his country into their own land, as was the promise of gathering them out of Assyria by Alexander the son of Antiochus Epiphanes. But it has its spiritual accomplishment in the gathering in of precious souls out of a bondage worse than that in Egypt or Assyria, and the bringing of them into the glorious liberties of the children of God and their enjoyments, which are as the beautiful fruitful pastures in <hi type="italic">the land of Gilead and Lebanon.</hi> All the land of promise is theirs, even Gilead, the utmost border of it eastward, and Lebanon, the utmost border northward. But how shall this be? How shall a people so dispersed be got together? How shall those that are set at such a distance from their own country be brought to it again? It is true the difficulties seem insuperable, but they shall be got over as easily, as effectually as those that lay in the way of their deliverance out of Egypt and their entrance into Canaan: <hi type="italic">He shall pass through the sea with affliction,</hi> as of old through the Red Sea, to the sore affliction of Pharaoh and his hosts, or to the sore affliction of the sea, the waves whereof <hi type="italic">he shall smite,</hi> so that it shall be <hi type="italic">driven back,</hi> as when <hi type="italic">the sea saw and fled,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ps.114.3">Ps. cxiv. 3</reference>. And <hi type="italic">all the deeps of the river</hi> (all the rivers, though ever so deep) <hi type="italic">shall dry up,</hi> as Jordan did, to make way for Israel's passage into that good land which God had given them. Does <hi type="italic">the pride of Assyria</hi> stand in the way of their deliverance? He shall give check to it who sets bounds to the <hi type="italic">proud waves of the sea,</hi> and it <hi type="italic">shall be brought down.</hi> Does the sceptre of Egypt oppose it? That shall <hi type="italic">depart away,</hi> so that it shall not be able to obstruct the gathering in of God's Israel when his time shall come for the doing of it. When the gospel-church was to be gathered out of all nations by the preaching of the gospel great opposition was given to it by the enraged combined powers of earth and hell. Insuperable difficulties seemed to be in the way of it. But, by a divine power going along with the doctrine of Christ, it became <hi type="italic">mighty to the pulling down of strong holds,</hi> and the conversion and salvation of thousands. Then the sea fled, and Jordan was <hi type="italic">driven back at the presence of the Lord.</hi> <div eID="gen20948" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20949" type="x-p"/> IV. They shall greatly multiply, and the church, that new world, shall be replenished (<reference osisRef="Zech.10.8">v. 8</reference>): <hi type="italic">They shall increase as they have increased</hi> formerly in Egypt, and great additions shall be made to their numbers, as in the days of David and Solomon. When God gathers his redeemed ones to himself they shall help to gather in others with them, and their motion homeward shall be like that of a snow-ball. <hi type="italic">Crescit eundo—The further it goes the larger it grows by accretion. I will gather them, and they shall increase.</hi> Note, The church of Christ is a growing body, as long as it is in the present state of minority, till it comes <hi type="italic">to the measure of the stature of the fulness of Christ.</hi> There are added to it <hi type="italic">daily such as shall be saved.</hi> 1. It shall spread to distant places. It shall fill Canaan, even to the lands of Gilead and Lebanon, so that no more place, no more room, shall be found for it there, <reference osisRef="Zech.10.10">v. 10</reference>. <hi type="italic">In Judah</hi> only <hi type="italic">God</hi> had been <hi type="italic">known,</hi> and his <hi type="italic">name was great in Israel</hi> only; here only he revealed his <hi type="italic">statutes</hi> and <hi type="italic">judgments.</hi> But in gospel-times that place shall be much too strait; the church's tent must be enlarged, and its <hi type="italic">cords lengthened:</hi> Then <hi type="italic">I will sow them among the people,</hi> <reference osisRef="Zech.10.9">v. 9</reference>. Their scattering shall be like the scattering of seed in the ground, not to bury it, but to increase it, that it may bring forth much fruit. The Jews are said to be dispersed <hi type="italic">into every nation under heaven</hi> (<reference osisRef="Acts.2.5">Acts ii. 5</reference>); and, as it was their troubles that dispersed some of them, so perhaps others transplanted themselves into colonies because the land of Israel was too strait for them; and many were natives of other nations, but proselyted to the Jewish religion. Now these were <hi type="italic">sown among the people,</hi> <reference osisRef="Hos.2.23">Hos. ii. 23</reference>. And this contributed very much to the spreading of the gospel. The Jews that came from all parts to worship at Jerusalem fetched thence the gospel light and fire to their own countries, as those <reference osisRef="Acts.2.1-Acts.2.47">Acts ii.</reference>, and the eunuch, <reference osisRef="Acts.8.26-Acts.8.40">Acts viii.</reference> And their own synagogues in the several cities of the Gentiles were the first receptacles of the apostles and their preaching, wherever they came. Thus when God <hi type="italic">sowed them among the people,</hi> that they might not get hurt by the Gentiles, but do good to them, he took care that they should <hi type="italic">remember him,</hi> and make mention of his name <hi type="italic">in far countries;</hi> and, by keeping up the knowledge of God among them as he had revealed himself in the Old Testament, they would be the more ready to admit the knowledge of Christ as he has revealed himself in the New Testament. 2. It shall last to future <hi type="italic">ages.</hi> The church shall not be <hi type="italic">res unius ætatis—a temporary thing,</hi> but a seed in it shall <hi type="italic">serve the Lord,</hi> <reference osisRef="Zech.10.7">v. 7</reference>. <hi type="italic">Yea, their children shall see it and be glad;</hi> and <hi type="italic">they shall live with their children, and turn again,</hi> <reference osisRef="Zech.10.9">v. 9</reference>. Converts to Christ shall have their children about them, whom they shall teach the knowledge of the Lord, and bring with them when they turn again to the holy land and the way of holiness. It was said to those to whom the gospel was first preached, <hi type="italic">The promise is to you and to your children,</hi> <reference osisRef="Acts.2.39">Acts ii. 39</reference>. They shall be <hi type="italic">so sown among the people</hi> as never to be extirpated. Christ's family upon earth shall never be extinct, nor his purchased possession lost for want of heirs. <div eID="gen20949" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20950" type="x-p"/> V. God himself will be both their strength and their song. 1. In him they shall be comforted, and shall have abundant satisfaction (<reference osisRef="Zech.10.7">v. 7</reference>): <hi type="italic">Their heart shall rejoice as through wine;</hi> for Christ's <hi type="italic">love,</hi> which is their joy, is <hi type="italic">better than wine.</hi> They shall be <hi type="italic">like a mighty man,</hi> and <hi type="italic">their heart shall rejoice.</hi> When we resolutely resist, and so overcome, our spiritual enemies, then our hearts shall rejoice. But we ruin our own joy if our resistance be feeble and we yield to the temptations of Satan. Their <hi type="italic">heart shall rejoice,</hi> and then they shall be as a <hi type="italic">mighty man;</hi> for the <hi type="italic">joy of the Lord</hi> will be <hi type="italic">our strength.</hi> And with their graces their joys shall be propagated: <hi type="italic">Their children shall see it and be glad, and their hearts</hi> also <hi type="italic">shall rejoice in the Lord.</hi> It is good to acquaint children betimes with the delights of religion, and to make the services of it as pleasant as may be to them, that, learning betimes to rejoice in the Lord, they may with purpose of heart cleave to him. 2. By him they shall be carried on with vigour, and enlargement of heart, in his service (<reference osisRef="Zech.10.12">v. 12</reference>): <hi type="italic">I will strengthen them in the Lord,</hi> strengthen them for their walk and work, as well as for their warfare. It is the God of Israel that <hi type="italic">gives strength and power unto his people,</hi> that strengthens all their powers and faculties for spiritual performances, above what they are by nature and against what they are by the corruption of nature. Now observe, (1.) How they are thus enabled and invigorated for their duty: <hi type="italic">I</hi> the Lord <hi type="italic">will strengthen them in the Lord,</hi> in the <hi type="italic">Messiah,</hi> who is <hi type="italic">Jehovah our strength,</hi> as well as <hi type="italic">Jehovah our righteousness.</hi> Strength is treasured up for us in Christ, and from him it is communicated to us. It is <hi type="italic">through Christ strengthening</hi> us that we can <hi type="italic">do all things,</hi> and <hi type="italic">without him we can do nothing.</hi> His <hi type="italic">strength is commanded</hi> him <hi type="italic">for this</hi> purpose, <reference osisRef="Ps.68.28">Ps. lxviii. 28</reference>. (2.) What good use they shall make of this strength given unto them: <hi type="italic">They shall walk up and down in his name.</hi> If God strengthen us, we must bestir ourselves, must <hi type="italic">walk up and down</hi> in all the duties of the Christian life, must be active and busy in the work of God, must walk up and down as industrious men do, losing no time, and letting slip no opportunity. But still we must <hi type="italic">walk up and down in the name of Christ,</hi> must do all by warrant from him and in dependence on him, with an eye to his word as our rule and his glory as our end. To us to live must be Christ; and, <hi type="italic">whatever we do in word or deed,</hi> we must <hi type="italic">do all in the name of the Lord Jesus,</hi> that we receive not the strengthening grace of God in vain. See <reference osisRef="Ps.80.17-Ps.80.18">Ps. lxxx. 17, 18</reference>.  <chapter eID="Zech.10"/> <div eID="gen20950" type="x-p"/>

entries.3cd75174200d05eb9eadc1112f6725277dfe6ddd: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv13140"/><title type="x-s2">CHAPTER 10</title> <title type="x-s3"><reference osisRef="Zech.10.1-Zech.10.12">Zec 10:1-12</reference>. Prayer and Promise.</title> <div sID="gen24750" type="x-p"/> Call to prayer to Jehovah, as contrasted with the idol-worship which had brought judgments on the princes and people. Blessings promised in answer to prayer: (1) rulers of themselves; (2) conquest of their enemies; (3) restoration and establishment of both Israel and Judah in their own land in lasting peace and piety.<div eID="gen24750" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24751" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv13140"/><hi type="bold">1. Ask ... rain--</hi>on which the abundance of "corn" promised by the Lord (<reference osisRef="Zech.9.17">Zec 9:17</reference>) depends. Jehovah alone can give it, and will give it on being asked (<reference osisRef="Jer.10.13">Jr 10:13</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jer.14.22">14:22</reference>).<div eID="gen24751" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24752" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">rain in ... time of ... latter rain--</hi>that is, the latter rain in its due time, namely, in spring, about February or March (<reference osisRef="Job.29.23">Job 29:23</reference>; <reference osisRef="Joel.2.23">Joe 2:23</reference>). The latter rain ripened the grain, as the former rain in October tended to fructify the seed. Including all temporal blessings; these again being types of spiritual ones. Though God has begun to bless us, we are not to relax our prayers. The former rain of conversion may have been given, but we must also ask for the latter rain of ripened sanctification. Though at Pentecost there was a former rain on the Jewish Church, a latter rain is still to be looked for, when the full harvest of the nation's conversion shall be gathered in to God. The spirit of prayer in the Church is an index at once of her piety, and of the spiritual blessings she may expect from God. When the Church is full of prayer, God pours out a full blessing.<div eID="gen24752" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24753" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">bright clouds--</hi>rather, "lightnings," the precursors of rain [Maurer].<div eID="gen24753" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24754" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">showers of rain--</hi>literally, "rain of heavy rain." In <reference osisRef="Job.37.6">Job 37:6</reference> the same words occur in inverted order [Henderson].<div eID="gen24754" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24755" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">grass--</hi>a general term, including both corn for men and grass for cattle. <div eID="gen24755" type="x-p"/>
entries.9b9e33cb4c4d1e4f02a706bf5c6d141bf9863dac: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv13141"/><div sID="gen24756" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv13141"/><hi type="bold">2. idols--</hi>literally, "the teraphim," the household gods, consulted in divination (see on <reference osisRef="Hos.3.4">Ho 3:4</reference>). Derived by Gesenius from an Arabic root, "comfort," indicating them as the givers of comfort. Or an Ethiopian root, "relics." Herein Zechariah shows that the Jews by their own idolatry had stayed the grace of God heretofore, which otherwise would have given them all those blessings, temporal and spiritual, which they are now (<reference osisRef="Zech.10.1">Zec 10:1</reference>) urged to "ask" for.<div eID="gen24756" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24757" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">diviners--</hi>who gave responses to consulters of the teraphim: opposed to Jehovah and His true prophets.<div eID="gen24757" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24758" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">seen a lie--</hi>pretending to see what they saw not in giving responses.<div eID="gen24758" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24759" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">comfort in vain--</hi>literally, "give vapor for comfort"; that is, give comforting promises to consulters which are sure to come to naught (<reference osisRef="Job.13.4">Job 13:4</reference>; <reference osisRef="Job.16.2">16:2</reference>; <reference osisRef="Job.21.34">21:34</reference>).<div eID="gen24759" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24760" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">therefore they went their way--</hi>that is, Israel and Judah were led away captive.<div eID="gen24760" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24761" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">as a flock ... no shepherd--</hi>As sheep wander and are a prey to every injury when without a shepherd, so the Jews had been while they were without Jehovah, the true shepherd; for the false prophets whom they trusted were no shepherds (<reference osisRef="Ezek.34.5">Eze 34:5</reference>). So now they are scattered, while they know not Messiah their shepherd; typified in the state of the disciples, when they had forsaken Jesus and fled (<reference osisRef="Matt.26.56">Mt 26:56</reference>; compare <reference osisRef="Zech.13.7">Zec 13:7</reference>). <div eID="gen24761" type="x-p"/>
entries.bb0abd326cf309b3908233a49c4ac8137aea1988: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv13142"/><div sID="gen24762" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv13142"/><hi type="bold">3. against the shepherds--</hi>the civil rulers of Israel and Judah who abetted idolatry.<div eID="gen24762" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24763" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">punished--</hi>literally, "visited upon." The same word "visited," without the upon, is presently after used in a good sense to heighten the contrast.<div eID="gen24763" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24764" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">goats--</hi>he-goats. As "shepherds" described what they ought to have been, so "he-goats" describes what they were, the emblem of headstrong wantonness and offensive lust (<reference osisRef="Isa.14.9">Is 14:9</reference>, Margin; <reference osisRef="Ezek.34.17">Eze 34:17</reference>; <reference osisRef="Dan.8.5">Da 8:5</reference>; <reference osisRef="Matt.25.33">Mt 25:33</reference>). The he-goats head the flock. They who are first in crime will be first in punishment.<div eID="gen24764" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24765" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">visited--</hi>in mercy (<reference osisRef="Luke.1.68">Lu 1:68</reference>).<div eID="gen24765" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24766" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">as his goodly horse--</hi>In <reference osisRef="Zech.9.13">Zec 9:13</reference> they were represented under the image of bows and arrows, here under that of their commander-in-chief, Jehovah's battle horse (<reference osisRef="Song.1.9">So 1:9</reference>). God can make His people, timid though they be as sheep, courageous as the charger. The general rode on the most beautiful and richly caparisoned, and had his horse tended with the greatest care. Jehovah might cast off the Jews for their vileness, but He regards His election or adoption of them: whence He calls them here "His flock," and therefore saves them. <div eID="gen24766" type="x-p"/>
entries.15f5043dd1ebd5ac2090a7d3d787f1cf2a42ef47: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv13143"/><div sID="gen24767" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv13143"/><hi type="bold">4. Out of him--</hi>Judah is to be no more subject to foreigners, but from itself shall come its rulers.<div eID="gen24767" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24768" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">the corner--</hi>stone, Messiah (<reference osisRef="Isa.28.16">Is 28:16</reference>). "Corners" simply express governors (<reference osisRef="1Sam.14.38">1Sa 14:38</reference>, Margin; <reference osisRef="Isa.19.13">Is 19:13</reference>, Margin). The Maccabees, Judah's governors and deliverers from Antiochus the oppressor, are primarily meant; but Messiah is the Antitype. Messiah supports and binds together the Church, Jews and Gentiles.<div eID="gen24768" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24769" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">the nail--</hi>(<reference osisRef="Judg.4.21">Jud 4:21</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.22.23">Is 22:23</reference>). The large peg inside an Oriental tent, on which is hung most of its valuable furniture. On Messiah hang all the glory and hope of His people.<div eID="gen24769" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24770" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">bow--</hi>(<reference osisRef="Zech.9.13">Zec 9:13</reference>). Judah shall not need foreign soldiery. Messiah shall be her battle-bow (<reference osisRef="Ps.45.4">Psa 45:4</reference>, <reference osisRef="Ps.45.5">5</reference>; <reference osisRef="Rev.6.2">Re 6:2</reference>).<div eID="gen24770" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24771" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">every oppressor--</hi>rather, in a good sense, ruler, as the kindred Ethiopic term means. So "exactor," in <reference osisRef="Isa.60.17">Is 60:17</reference>, namely, one who exacts the tribute from the nations made tributary to Judah [Ludovicus De Dieu]. <div eID="gen24771" type="x-p"/>
entries.5dabb30798e2b7fdd333da7828a6ac58cc918381: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv13144"/><div sID="gen24772" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv13144"/><hi type="bold">5. riders on horses--</hi>namely, the enemy's horsemen. Though the Jews were forbidden by the law to multiply horses in battle (<reference osisRef="Deut.17.16">De 17:16</reference>), they are made Jehovah's war horse (<reference osisRef="Zech.10.3">Zec 10:3</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.20.7">Psa 20:7</reference>), and so tread down on foot the foe with all his cavalry (<reference osisRef="Ezek.38.4">Eze 38:4</reference>; <reference osisRef="Dan.11.40">Da 11:40</reference>). Cavalry was the chief strength of the Syro-Grecian army (1 Maccabees 3:39). <div eID="gen24772" type="x-p"/>
entries.ce2c345a8681fbf90b0ebe2ac71ac604d02b402b: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv13145"/><div sID="gen24773" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv13145"/><hi type="bold">6. Judah ... Joseph--</hi>that is, the ten tribes. The distinct mention of both Judah and Israel shows that there is yet a more complete restoration than that from Babylon, when Judah alone and a few Israelites from the other tribes returned. The Maccabean deliverance is here connected with it, just as the painter groups on the same canvas objects in the foreground and hills far distant; or as the comparatively near planet and the remote fixed star are seen together in the same firmament. Prophecy ever hastens to the glorious final consummation under Messiah.<div eID="gen24773" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24774" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">bring them again to place them--</hi>namely, securely in their own land. The Hebrew verb is compounded of two, "I will bring again," and "I will place them" (<reference osisRef="Jer.32.37">Jr 32:37</reference>). Maurer, from a different form, translates, "I will make them to dwell." <div eID="gen24774" type="x-p"/>
entries.761801d816e9f8b56db80646d2d625ad3f43db27: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv13146"/><div sID="gen24775" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv13146"/><hi type="bold">7. like a mighty man--</hi>in the battle with the foe (<reference osisRef="Zech.10.3">Zec 10:3</reference>, <reference osisRef="Zech.10.5">5</reference>).<div eID="gen24775" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24776" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">rejoice--</hi>at their victory over the foe.<div eID="gen24776" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24777" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">children shall see it--</hi>who are not yet of age to serve. To teach patient waiting for God's promises. If ye do not at present see the fulfilment, your children shall, and their joy shall be complete.<div eID="gen24777" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24778" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">rejoice in the Lord--</hi>the Giver of such a glorious victory. <div eID="gen24778" type="x-p"/>
entries.d497d91302431f63c3097b72346aadf1c9939dff: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv13147"/><div sID="gen24779" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv13147"/><hi type="bold">8. hiss for them--</hi>Keepers of bees by a whistle call them together. So Jehovah by the mere word of His call shall gather back to Palestine His scattered people (<reference osisRef="Zech.10.10">Zec 10:10</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.5.26">Is 5:26</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ezek.36.11">Eze 36:11</reference>). The multitudes mentioned by Josephus [Wars of the Jews, 3:2], as peopling Galilee two hundred years after this time, were a pledge of the future more perfect fulfilment of the prophecy.<div eID="gen24779" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24780" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">for I have redeemed them--</hi>namely, in My covenant purpose "redeemed" both temporally and spiritually.<div eID="gen24780" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24781" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">as they have increased--</hi>in former times. <div eID="gen24781" type="x-p"/>
entries.2ed9760950bb7ed13cd03effe8527c25fb56a06b: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv13148"/><div sID="gen24782" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv13148"/><hi type="bold">9. sow them among ... people--</hi>Their dispersion was with a special design. Like seed sown far and wide, they shall, when quickened themselves, be the fittest instruments for quickening others (compare <reference osisRef="Mic.5.7">Mi 5:7</reference>). The slight hold they have on every soil where they now live, as also the commercial and therefore cosmopolitan character of their pursuits, making a change of residence easy to them, fit them peculiarly for missionary work [Moore]. The wide dispersion of the Jews just before Christ's coming prepared the way similarly for the apostles' preaching in the various Jewish synagogues throughout the world; everywhere some of the Old Testament seed previously sown was ready to germinate when the New Testament light and heat were brought to bear on it by Gospel preachers. Thus the way was opened for entrance among the Gentiles. "Will sow" is the Hebrew future, said of that which has been done, is being done, and may be done afterwards [Maurer], (compare <reference osisRef="Hos.2.23">Ho 2:23</reference>).<div eID="gen24782" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24783" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">shall remember me in far countries--</hi>(<reference osisRef="Deut.30.1">De 30:1</reference>; <reference osisRef="2Chr.6.37">2Ch 6:37</reference>). Implying the Jews' return to a right mind in "all the nations" where they are scattered simultaneously. Compare <reference osisRef="Luke.15.17">Lu 15:17</reference>, <reference osisRef="Luke.15.18">18</reference>, with <reference osisRef="Ps.22.27">Psa 22:27</reference>, "All the ends of the world remembering and turning unto the Lord," preceded by the "seed of Jacob ... Israel ... fearing and glorifying Him"; also <reference osisRef="Ps.102.13-Ps.102.15">Psa 102:13-15</reference>.<div eID="gen24783" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24784" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">live--</hi>in political and spiritual life. <div eID="gen24784" type="x-p"/>
entries.4f247c1ea3357ce27833369a7856110653fb5151: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv13149"/><div sID="gen24785" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv13149"/><hi type="bold">10. Egypt ... Assyria--</hi>the former the first, the latter among the last of Israel's oppressors (or representing the four great world kingdoms, of which it was the first): types of the present universal dispersion, Egypt being south, Assyria north, opposite ends of the compass. Maurer conjectures that many Israelites fled to "Egypt" on the invasion of Tiglath-pileser. But <reference osisRef="Isa.11.11">Is 11:11</reference> and this passage rather accord with the view of the future restoration.<div eID="gen24785" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24786" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">Gilead ... Lebanon--</hi>The whole of the Holy Land is described by two of its boundaries, the eastern ("Gilead" beyond Jordan) and the northern ("Lebanon").<div eID="gen24786" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24787" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">place shall not be found for them--</hi>that is, there shall not be room enough for them through their numbers (<reference osisRef="Isa.49.20">Is 49:20</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.54.3">54:3</reference>). <div eID="gen24787" type="x-p"/>
entries.1481833f35729f52c8d9d2bf02bc54b28d5f1012: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv13150"/><div sID="gen24788" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv13150"/><hi type="bold">11. pass ... sea with affliction--</hi>Personifying the "sea"; He shall afflict the sea, that is, cause it to cease to be an obstacle to Israel's return to Palestine (<reference osisRef="Isa.11.15">Is 11:15</reference>, <reference osisRef="Isa.11.16">16</reference>). Vulgate translates, "The strait of the sea." Maurer, "He shall cleave and smite." English Version is best (<reference osisRef="Ps.114.3">Psa 114:3</reference>). As Jehovah smote the Red Sea to make a passage for His people (<reference osisRef="Exod.14.16">Ex 14:16</reference>, <reference osisRef="Exod.14.21">21</reference>), so hereafter shall He make a way through every obstacle which opposes Israel's restoration.<div eID="gen24788" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24789" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">the river--</hi>the Nile (<reference osisRef="Amos.8.8">Am 8:8</reference>; <reference osisRef="Amos.9.5">9:5</reference>), or the Euphrates. Thus the Red Sea and the Euphrates in the former part of the verse answer to "Assyria" and "Egypt" in the latter.<div eID="gen24789" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24790" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">sceptre of Egypt ... depart--</hi>(<reference osisRef="Ezek.30.13">Eze 30:13</reference>). <div eID="gen24790" type="x-p"/>
entries.2cb80c2c49c4783dd5a470973a4bd8711746e9ba: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv13151"/><div sID="gen24791" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv13151"/><hi type="bold">12. I ... strengthen them in ... Lord--</hi>(<reference osisRef="Hos.1.7">Ho 1:7</reference>). I, the Father, will strengthen them in the name, that is, the manifested power, of the Lord, Messiah, the Son of God.<div eID="gen24791" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24792" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">walk ... in his name--</hi>that is, live everywhere and continually under His protection, and according to His will (<reference osisRef="Gen.5.22">Ge 5:22</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.20.1">Psa 20:1</reference>, <reference osisRef="Ps.20.7">7</reference>; <reference osisRef="Mic.4.5">Mi 4:5</reference>). <chapter eID="Zech.10"/>

entries.122df9e7e9d75ff03cba66bdab5b1d5ad9aa56d1: <div eID="gen35657" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s">Introduction</title> <div sID="gen35658" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen35659" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen35659" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen35658" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen35660" type="x-p"/> The promise of prosperity and plenty in the close of the preceding chapter leads the prophet to suggest, next, the means of obtaining them; supplication to Jehovah, and not to idols, whose worship had already proved a fertile source of calamities, <reference osisRef="Zac.10.1-Zac.10.3">Zac 10:1-3</reference>. The rest of the chapter (like the preceding) promises to the Jews a restoration to their own land under rulers and governors, victory over their enemies, and much increase and prosperity; and this in a manner so miraculous, that it is described, <reference osisRef="Zac.10.4-Zac.10.12">Zac 10:4-12</reference>, by allusions to the deliverance from Egypt. <div eID="gen35660" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen35661" type="x-p"/> <hi type="bold">Verse 1</hi> <div eID="gen35661" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen35662" type="x-p"/> Ask ye of the Lord rain - Rain in the due seasons - <div eID="gen35662" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen35663" type="x-p"/> 1. To impregnate the seed when sown; and <div eID="gen35663" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen35664" type="x-p"/> 2. To fill the ear near the time of harvest - was so essential to the fertility of the land, and the well-being of the people, that it stands well among the chief of God's mercies and the promise of it here shows that God designs to ensure the prosperity promised, by using those means by which it was promoted.
entries.93809ea95fe1bcc3917451a444a32d5e8aee0df8: <hi type="bold">Verse 2</hi> <div eID="gen35664" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen35665" type="x-p"/> The idols have spoken vanity - This is spoken of the Jews, and must refer to their idolatry practiced before the captivity, for there were no idols after. <div eID="gen35665" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen35666" type="x-p"/> Therefore they went their way - They were like a flock that had no shepherd, shifting from place to place, and wandering about in the wilderness, seeking for pasture, wherever they might find it. Some think that the idols and diviners were those of the Seleucidae Greeks, who excited their masters with promises of success against the Maccabees. Others think that the Babylonish captivity is foretold; for a determined future event is frequently spoken of by the prophets as past.
entries.327124d333d57678123221bb3ba8fa464588e562: <hi type="bold">Verse 3</hi> <div eID="gen35666" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen35667" type="x-p"/> Mine anger was kindled against the shepherds - Bad kings and bad priests. I will punish the goats; these were the wicked priests, who were shepherds by their office, and goats by the impurity of their lives. <div eID="gen35667" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen35668" type="x-p"/> As his goodly horse in the battle - The honorable war horse, or the horse that carried the general's equipage. In the unaccountable variation of interpreters on these chapters, this, among other things, is thought to be spoken of Matthias, and Judas Maccabeus, who assembled the people from all quarters, as a shepherd gathers his sheep together; and led them against the sons of Greece, the Seleucidae Greeks. Others refer every thing here to times before the captivity.
entries.64c7df92fbc15cc97984b171306176c5e80aaf3c: <hi type="bold">Verse 4</hi> <div eID="gen35668" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen35669" type="x-p"/> Out of him came forth the corner - This is spoken of the tribe of Judah: all strength, counsel, and excellence came from that tribe. The corner stone, the ornament and completion of the building; the nail, by which the tents were fastened, and on which they hung their clothes, armor, etc., the battlebow, the choicest archers. <div eID="gen35669" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen35670" type="x-p"/> Every oppressor together - Those heroes and generals, by whom, under God, their foes should be totally routed. Newcome translates, "Every ruler together." Perhaps all this is spoken of the Messiah.
entries.69539fae45a233b8fff3b53381e4a41ce89d287f: <hi type="bold">Verse 5</hi> <div eID="gen35670" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen35671" type="x-p"/> They shall be as mighty men - The Maccabees and their successors. <div eID="gen35671" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen35672" type="x-p"/> Riders on horses - The Macedonians, who opposed the Maccabees, and had much cavalry; whereas the Jews had none, and even few weapons of war; yet they overcame these horsemen.
entries.afa106effa0a7da3de02b84cc0df25b33b9b7c06: <hi type="bold">Verse 6</hi> <div eID="gen35672" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen35673" type="x-p"/> I will strengthen the house of Judah - I doubt whether the sixth, seventh, eighth, and ninth verses are not to be understood of the future ingathering of the Jews in the times of the Gospel. See <reference osisRef="Jer.3.14">Jer 3:14</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jer.23.6">Jer 23:6</reference>; <reference osisRef="Hos.1.2">Hos 1:2</reference>; <reference osisRef="Hos.6.11">Hos 6:11</reference>.
entries.25e8abc67bea7fc0de248389d792a9d597a753f9: <hi type="bold">Verse 7</hi> <div eID="gen35673" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen35674" type="x-p"/> Ephraim shall be like a mighty man - This tribe was always distinguished for its valor.
entries.00ab210daffeba18625595602d0183fef126781a: <hi type="bold">Verse 8</hi> <div eID="gen35674" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen35675" type="x-p"/> I will hiss for them - אשרקה eshrekah, "I will shriek for them;" call them with such a shrill strong voice, that they shall hear me, and find that it is the voice of their redemption.
entries.6a0688f61c5190d88c55b6932999728592b178fd: <hi type="bold">Verse 9</hi> <div eID="gen35675" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen35676" type="x-p"/> I will sow them among the people - Wherever they have been dispersed, my voice in the preaching of the Gospel shall reach them. And they shall remember me, and they and their children shall turn again to the Lord, through Messiah their King.
entries.9b5dfd2f90f51c9bf165a41db971cdd6595a52e3: <hi type="bold">Verse 10</hi> <div eID="gen35676" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen35677" type="x-p"/> Out of the land of Egypt - I will bring them out of all the countries where they have been dispersed, and bring them back to their own land; and they shall be so numerous that they shall scarcely find there, in all its length and breadth, a sufficiency of room. If all the Jews that are now scattered over the face of the earth were gathered together, they would make a mighty nation. And God will gather them together. As a wonderful providence has preserved them in every place, so a wondrous providence will collect them from every place of their dispersion. When the great call comes, no one soul of them shall be left behind.
entries.017c09cba30022c77fb3a8b418d925bb55fc1899: <hi type="bold">Verse 11</hi> <div eID="gen35677" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen35678" type="x-p"/> And he shall pass through the sea - Here is an allusion to the passage of the Red Sea, on their coming out of Egypt, and to their crossing Jordan, when they went into the promised land; the waves or waters of both were dried up, thrown from side to side, till all the people passed safely through. When they shall return from the various countries in which they now sojourn, God will work, if necessary, similar miracles to those which he formerly worked for their forefathers; and the people shall be glad to let them go, however much they may be profited by their operations in the state. Those that oppose, as Assyria and Egypt formerly did, shall be brought down, and their scepter broken.
entries.f672e214963ae44b3928a799ba8f855381456657: <hi type="bold">Verse 12</hi> <div eID="gen35678" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen35679" type="x-p"/> I will strengthen them in the Lord - I, the God of Israel, will strengthen them in the Lord-Jesus, the Messiah; and thus indeed the Chaldee: I will strengthen them, בימרא דיי bemeymre dayai, in or by the Word of Jehovah, the same personal Word which we so often meet with in the Chaldee paraphrases or Targum. <div eID="gen35679" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen35680" type="x-p"/> They shall walk up and down in his name - In the name of the Messiah. Saith the Lord - God speaks here, not of himself, but concerning his Christ. The Jews shall have complete liberty; they shall appear everywhere as a part of the flock of Christ, and no difference be made between them and the converted Gentiles. They shall be all one fold under one Shepherd and Bishop of all souls.  <chapter eID="Zech.10"/> <div eID="gen35680" type="x-p"/>

entries.2d9828db9447def407c91e00b28826d25bc35348: Zec 10:1-2 <hi type="italic">“Ask ye of Jehovah rain in the time of the latter rain; Jehovah createth lightnings, and showers of rain will He give them, to every one vegetation in the field.</hi> Zec 10:2. <hi type="italic">For the teraphim have spoken vanity, and the soothsayers have seen a lie, and speak dreams of deceit; they comfort in vain: for this they have wandered like a flock, they are oppressed because there is no shepherd.” </hi> The summons to prayer is not a mere turn of the address expressing the readiness of God to give (Hengstenberg), but is seriously meant, as the reason assigned in Zec 10:2 clearly shows. The church of the Lord is to ask of God the blessings which it needs for its prosperity, and not to put its trust in idols, as rebellious Israel has done (Hos 2:7). The prayer for rain, on which the successful cultivation of the fruits of the ground depends, simply serves to individualize the prayer for the bestowal of the blessings of God, in order to sustain both temporal and spiritual life; just as in Zec 9:17 the fruitfulness of the land and the flourishing of the nation are simply a concrete expression, for the whole complex of the salvation which the Lord will grant to His people (Kliefoth). This view, which answers to the rhetorical character of the exhortation, is very different from allegory. The time of the latter rain is mentioned, because this was indispensable to the ripening of the corn, whereas elsewhere the early and latter rain are connected together (e.g., <reference osisRef="Joel.2.23">Joe 2:23</reference>; <reference osisRef="Deut.11.13-Deut.11.15">Deu 11:13-15</reference>). The lightnings are introduced as the harbingers of rain (cf. <reference osisRef="Jer.10.13">Jer 10:13</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.135.7">Psa 135:7</reference>). <hi type="italic">Metar geshem</hi>, rain of the rain-pouring, i.e., copious rain (compare <reference osisRef="Job.37.6">Job 37:6</reference>, where the words are transposed). With <hi type="italic">lâkem</hi> (to them) the address passes into the third person: to them, i.e., to every one who asks. עשׂב is not to be restricted to grass or herb as the food of cattle, as in <reference osisRef="Deut.11.15">Deu 11:15</reference>, where it is mentioned in connection with the corn and the fruits of the field; but it includes these, as in <reference osisRef="Gen.1.29">Gen 1:29</reference> and <reference osisRef="Ps.104.14">Psa 104:14</reference>, where it is distinguished from <hi type="italic">châtsı̄r</hi>. The exhortation to pray to Jehovah for the blessing needed to ensure prosperity, is supported in Zec 10:2 by an allusion to the worthlessness of the trust in idols, and to the misery which idolatry with its consequences, viz., soothsaying and false prophecy, have brought upon the nation. The <hi type="italic">terâphı̄m</hi> were house-deities and oracular deities, which were worshipped as the givers and protectors of the blessings of earthly prosperity (see at <reference osisRef="Gen.31.19">Gen 31:19</reference>). Along with these קוסמים are mentioned, i.e., the soothsayers, who plunged the nation into misery through their vain and deceitful prophesyings. חלמות is not the subject of the sentence, for in that case it would have the article like הקּוסמים; but it is the object, and הקּוסמים is also the subject to ידבּרוּ and ינחמוּן. “Therefore,” i.e., because Israel had trusted in teraphim and soothsayers, it would have to wander into exile. נסע, to break up, applied to the pulling up of the pegs, to take down the tent, involves the idea of wandering, and in this connection, of wandering into exile. Hence the perfect נסעוּ, to which the imperfect יענוּ is suitably appended, because their being oppressed, i.e., the oppression which Israel suffered from the heathen, still continued. The words apply of course to all Israel (Ephraim and Judah); compare Zec 9:13 with Zec 10:4, Zec 10:6. Israel is bowed down because it has no shepherd, i.e., no king, who guards and provides for his people (cf. Num 27:17; <reference osisRef="Jer.23.4">Jer 23:4</reference>), having lost the Davidic monarchy when the kingdom was overthrown.
entries.72b3c8cc5c25952982462c6334e8f4aefdb55dc9: Zec 10:3-4 <div eID="gen16885" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16886" type="x-p"/> To this there is appended in Zec 10:3. the promise that Jehovah will take possession of His flock, and redeem it out of the oppression of the evil shepherds. Zec 10:3. <hi type="italic">“My wrath is kindled upon the shepherds, and the goats shall I punish; for Jehovah of hosts visits His flock, the house of Judah, and makes it like His state-horse in the war.</hi> Zec 10:4. <hi type="italic">From Him will be corner-stone, from Him the nail, from Him the war-bow; from Him will every ruler go forth at once.” </hi> When Israel lost its own shepherds, it came under the tyranny of bad shepherds. These were the heathen governors and tyrants. Against these the wrath of Jehovah is kindled, and He will punish them. There is no material difference between רעים, shepherds, and עתּוּדים, leading goats. <hi type="italic">‛Attūdı̄m</hi> also signifies rulers, as in Isa 14:9. The reason assigned why the evil shepherds are to be punished, is that Jehovah visits His flock. The perfect <hi type="italic">pâqad</hi> is used prophetically of what God has resolved to do, and will actually carry out; and <hi type="italic">pâqad</hi> <hi type="italic">c. acc. pers.</hi> means to visit, i.e., to assume the care of, as distinguished from <hi type="italic">pâqad</hi> with <hi type="italic">'al pers.</hi>, to visit in the sense of to punish (see at Zep 2:7). The house of Judah only is mentioned in Zec 10:3, not in distinction from Ephraim, however (cf. Zec 10:6), but as the stem and kernel of the covenant nation, with which Ephraim is to be united once more. The care of God for Judah will not be limited to its liberation from the oppression of the bad shepherds; but Jehovah will also make Judah into a victorious people. This is the meaning of the figure “like a state-horse,” i.e., a splendid and richly ornamented war-horse, such as a king is accustomed to ride. This figure is not more striking than the description of Judah and Ephraim as a bow and arrow (Zec 9:13). This equipment of Judah as a warlike power overcoming its foes is described in Zec 10:4, namely in 4 <hi type="italic">a</hi>, in figures taken from the firmness and furnishing of a house with everything requisite, and in 4 <hi type="italic">b</hi>, etc., in literal words. The verb יצא of the fourth clause cannot be taken as the verb belonging to the ממּנּוּ in the first three clauses, because יצא is neither applicable to <hi type="italic">pinnâh</hi> nor to <hi type="italic">yâthēd</hi>. We have therefore to supply יהיה. From (out of) Him will be <hi type="italic">pinnâh</hi>, corner, here corner-stone, as in <reference osisRef="Isa.28.16">Isa 28:16</reference>, upon which the whole building stands firmly, and will be built securely, - a suitable figure for the firm, stately foundation which Judah is to receive. To this is added <hi type="italic">yâthēd</hi>, the plug. This figure is to be explained from the arrangement of eastern houses, in which the inner walls are provided with a row of large nails or plugs for hanging the house utensils upon. The plug, therefore, is a suitable figure for the supports or upholders of the whole political constitution, and even in <reference osisRef="Isa.22.23">Isa 22:23</reference> was transferred to persons. The war-bow stands synecdochically for weapons of war and the military power. It is a disputed point, however, whether the suffix in <hi type="italic">mimmennū</hi> (out of him) refers to <hi type="italic">Judah</hi> or <hi type="italic">Jehovah</hi>. But the opinion of Hitzig and others, that it refers to Jehovah, is overthrown by the expression יצא ממּנּוּ in the last clause. For even if we could say, Judah will receive its firm foundation, its internal fortification, and its military strength from <hi type="italic">Jehovah</hi>, the expression, “Every military commander will go out or come forth out of Jehovah,” is unheard-of and unscriptural. It is not affirmed in the Old Testament even of the Messiah that He goes forth out of God, although His “goings forth” are from eternity (Mic 5:1), and He Himself is called <hi type="italic">El gibbōr</hi> (<reference osisRef="Isa.9.5">Isa 9:5</reference>). Still less can this be affirmed of <hi type="italic">every</hi> ruler (<hi type="italic">kol</hi>-<hi type="italic">mōgēs</hi>) of Judah. In this clause, therefore, <hi type="italic">mimmennū</hi> must refer to Judah, and consequently it must be taken in the same way in the first three clauses. On יצא מן, see Mic 5:1. <hi type="italic">Nōgēs</hi>, an oppressor or taskmaster, is not applied to a leader or ruler in a good sense even here, any more than in <reference osisRef="Isa.3.12">Isa 3:12</reference> and <reference osisRef="Isa.60.17">Isa 60:17</reference> (see the comm. on these passages). The fact that <hi type="italic">negus</hi> in Ethiopic is the name given to the king (Koehler), proves nothing in relation to Hebrew usage. The word has the subordinate idea of oppressor, or despotic ruler, in this instance also; but the idea of harshness refers not to the covenant nation, but to its enemies (Hengstenberg), and the words are used in antithesis to Zec 9:8. Whereas there the promise is given to the nation of Israel that it will not fall under the power of the <hi type="italic">nōgēs</hi> any more, it is here assured that it is to attain to the position of a <hi type="italic">nōgēs</hi> in relation to its foes (Kliefoth). כּל־נוגשׂ is strengthened by יחדּו: every oppressor together, which Judah will require in opposition to its foes.
entries.eaec5defccc8f197206f52796ace9a983303e1af: Zec 10:5-7 <div eID="gen16886" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16887" type="x-p"/> Thus equipped for battle, Judah will annihilate its foes. Zec 10:5. <hi type="italic">“And they will be like heroes, treading street-mire in the battle: and will fight, for Jehovah is with them, and the riders upon horses are put to shame.</hi> Zec 10:6. <hi type="italic">And I shall strengthen the house of Judah, and grant salvation to the house of Joseph, and shall make them dwell; for I have had compassion upon them: and they will be as if I had not rejected them: for I am Jehovah their God, and will hear them.</hi> Zec 10:7. <hi type="italic">And Ephraim will be like a hero, and their heart will rejoice as if with wine: and their children will see it, and rejoice; their heart shall rejoice in Jehovah.” </hi> In Zec 10:5, <hi type="italic">bōsı̄m</hi> is a more precise definition of <hi type="italic">kegibbōrı̄m</hi>, and the house of Judah (Zec 10:3) is the subject of the sentence. They will be like heroes, namely, treading upon mire. <hi type="italic">Bōsı̄m</hi> is the <hi type="italic">kal</hi> participle used in an intransitive sense, since the form with <hi type="italic">o</hi> only occurs in verbs with an intransitive meaning, like <hi type="italic">bōsh</hi>, <hi type="italic">lōt</hi>, <hi type="italic">qōm</hi>; and <hi type="italic">būs</hi> in <hi type="italic">kal</hi> is construed in every other case with the accusative of the object: treading upon mire = treading or treading down mire. Consequently the object which they tread down or trample in pieces is expressed by בּטיט חוּצות; and thus the arbitrary completion of the sentence by “everything that opposes them” (C. B. Mich. and Koehler) is set aside as untenable. Now, as “treading upon mire” cannot possibly express merely the firm tread of a courageous man (Hitzig), we must take the dirt of the streets as a figurative expression for the enemy, and the phrase “treading upon street-mire” as a bold figure denoting the trampling down of the enemy in the mire of the streets (Mic 7:10; <reference osisRef="2Sam.22.43">2Sa 22:43</reference>), analogous to their “treading down sling-stones,” Zec 9:15. For such heroic conflict will they be fitted by the help of Jehovah, that the enemy will be put to shame before them. The riders of the horses are mentioned for the purpose of individualizing the enemy, because the principal strength of the Asiatic rulers consisted in cavalry (see <reference osisRef="Dan.11.40">Dan 11:40</reference>). הובישׁ intransitive, as in Zec 9:5. This strength for a victorious conflict will not be confined to Judah, but Ephraim will also share it. The words, “and the house of Ephraim will I endow with salvation,” have been taken by Koehler as signifying “that Jehovah will deliver the house of Ephraim by granting the victory to the house of Judah in conflict with its own foes and those of Ephraim also;” but there is no ground for this. We may see from Zec 10:7, according to which Ephraim will also fight as a hero, as Judah will according to Zec 10:5, that הושׁיע does not mean merely to help or deliver, but to grant salvation, as in Zec 9:16. The circumstance, however, “that in the course of the chapter, at any rate from Zec 10:7 onwards, it is only Ephraim whose deliverance and restoration are spoken of,” proves nothing more than that Ephraim will receive the same salvation as Judah, but not that it will be delivered by the house of Judah. The abnormal form הושׁבותים is regarded by many, who follow Kimchi and Aben Ezra, as a <hi type="italic">forma composita </hi>from הושׁבתּים and השׁיבותי: “I make them dwell, and bring them back.” But this is precluded by the fact that the bringing back would necessarily precede the making to dwell, to say nothing of the circumstance that there is no analogy whatever for such a composition (cf. <reference osisRef="Jer.32.37">Jer 32:37</reference>). The form is rather to be explained from a confusion of the verbs עו and פי, and is the <hi type="italic">hiphil</hi> of ישׁב for הושׁבתּים (lxx, Maurer, Hengstenberg; comp. Olshausen, <hi type="italic">Grammat.</hi> p. 559), and not a <hi type="italic">hiphil</hi> of שׁוּב, in which a transition has taken place into the <hi type="italic">hiphil</hi> form of the verbs פו (Ewald, §196, <hi type="italic">b</hi>, Not. 1; Targ., Vulg., Hitzig, and Koehler). For “bringing back” affirms too little here. הושׁבתּים, “I make them dwell,” corresponds rather to “they shall be as if they had not been cast off,” without needing any further definition, since not only do we meet with ישׁב without anything else, in the sense of peaceful, happy dwelling (e.g., Mic 5:3), but here also the manner of dwelling is indicated in the appended clause כּאשׁר לא־זנחתּים, “as before they were cast off” (cf. <reference osisRef="Ezek.36.11">Eze 36:11</reference>). אענם is also not to be taken as referring to the answering of the prayers, which Ephraim addressed to Jehovah out of its distress, out of its imprisonment (Koehler), but is to be taken in a much more general sense, as in Zec 13:9; <reference osisRef="Isa.58.9">Isa 58:9</reference>, and Hos 2:23. Ephraim, like Judah, will also become a hero, and rejoice as if with wine, i.e., fight joyfully like a hero strengthened with wine (cf. <reference osisRef="Ps.78.65-Ps.78.66">Psa 78:65-66</reference>). This rejoicing in conflict the sons will see, and exult in consequence; so that it will be a lasting joy.
entries.1cfd02c474f5d8cedb835ac69cfbac035c80f1a8: Zec 10:8-10 <div eID="gen16887" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16888" type="x-p"/> In order to remove all doubt as to the realization of this promise, the deliverance of Ephraim is described still more minutely in Zec 10:8-12. Zec 10:8. <hi type="italic">“I will hiss to them, and gather them; for I have redeemed them: and they will multiply as they have multiplied.</hi> Zec 10:9. <hi type="italic">And I will sow them among the nations: and in the far-off lands will they remember me; and will live with their sons, and return.</hi> Zec 10:10. <hi type="italic">And I will bring them back out of the land of Egypt, and gather them out of Asshur, and bring them into the land of Gilead and of Lebanon; and room will not be found for them.” </hi> That these verses do not treat of a fresh (second) dispersion of Ephraim, or represent the carrying away as still in the future (Hitzig), is evident from the words themselves, when correctly interpreted. Not only are the enticing and gathering together (Zec 10:8) mentioned before the sowing or dispersing (Zec 10:9), but they are both expressed by similar verbal forms (אשׁרקה and אזרעם); and the misinterpretation is thereby precluded, that events occurring at different times are referred to. We must also observe the voluntative form אשׁרקה, “I will (not I shall) hiss to them, i.e., entice them” (<hi type="italic">shâraq</hi> being used for alluring, as in <reference osisRef="Isa.5.26">Isa 5:26</reference> and <reference osisRef="Isa.7.18">Isa 7:18</reference>), as well as the absence of a copula. They both show that the intention here is simply to explain with greater clearness what is announced in Zec 10:6, Zec 10:7. The perfect פּדיתים is prophetic, like רחמתּים in Zec 10:6. The further promise, “they will multiply,” etc., cannot be taken as referring either merely to the multiplication of Israel in exile (Hengst., Koehler, etc.), or merely to the future multiplication after the gathering together. According to the position in which the words stand between אקבּצם and אזרעם, they must embrace both the multiplication during the dispersion, and the multiplication after the gathering together. The perfect כּמו רבוּ points to the increase which Israel experienced in the olden time under the oppression of Egypt (<reference osisRef="Exod.1.7">Exo 1:7</reference>, <reference osisRef="Exod.1.12">Exo 1:12</reference>). This increase, which is also promised in <reference osisRef="Ezek.36.10-Ezek.36.11">Eze 36:10-11</reference>, is effected by God’s sowing them broadcast among the nations. זרע does not mean to scatter, but to sow, to sow broadcast (see at Hos 2:23). Consequently the reference cannot be to a dispersion of Israel inflicted as a punishment. The sowing denotes the multiplication (cf. <reference osisRef="Jer.31.27">Jer 31:27</reference>), and is not to be interpreted, as Neumann and Kliefoth suppose, as signifying that the Ephraimites are to be scattered as seed-corn among the heathen, to spread the knowledge of Jehovah among the nations. This thought is quite foreign to the context; and even in the words, “in far-off lands will they remember me,” it is neither expressed nor implied. These words are to be connected with what follows: Because they remember the Lord in far-off lands, they will live, and return with their children. In <hi type="italic">Zec 10:10</hi> the gathering together and leading back of Israel are more minutely described, and indeed as taking place out of the land of Asshur and out of Egypt. The fact that these two lands are mentioned, upon which modern critics have principally founded their arguments in favour of the origin of this prophecy before the captivity, cannot be explained “from the circumstance that in the time of Tiglath-pileser and Shalmaneser many Ephraimites had fled to Egypt” (Koehler and others); for history knows nothing of this, and the supposition is merely a loophole for escaping from a difficulty. Such passages as Hos 8:13; Hos 9:3, Hos 9:6; Hos 11:11; Mic 7:12; <reference osisRef="Isa.11.11">Isa 11:11</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.27.13">Isa 27:13</reference>, furnish no historical evidence of such thing. Even if certain Ephraimites had fled to Egypt, these could not be explained as relating to a return or gathering together of the Ephraimites of Israelites out of Egypt and Assyria, because the announcement presupposes that the Ephraimites had been transported to Egypt in quite as large numbers as to Assyria, - a fact which cannot be established either in relation to the times before or to those after the captivity. Egypt, as we have already shown at Hos 9:3 (cf. Zec 8:13), is rather introduced in all the passages mentioned simply as a type of the land of bondage, on account of its having been the land in which Israel lived in the olden time, under the oppression of the heathen world. And Asshur is introduced in the same way, as the land into which the ten tribes had been afterwards exiled. This typical significance is placed beyond all doubt by Zec 10:1, since the redemption of Israel out of the countries named is there exhibited under the type of the liberation of Israel out of the bondage of Egypt under the guidance of Moses. (Compare also Delitzsch on Isa 11:11.) The Ephraimites are to return into the land of Gilead and Lebanon; the former representing the territory of the ten tribes in the olden time to the east of the Jordan, the latter that to the west (cf. Mic 7:14). לא ימּצא, there is not found for them, sc. the necessary room: equivalent to, it will not be sufficient for them (as in <reference osisRef="Josh.17.16">Jos 17:16</reference>).
entries.5da2cd7cb1ed8ddf769c70f8486d25abd275d838: Zec 10:11-12 <div eID="gen16888" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16889" type="x-p"/> Zec 10:11. <hi type="italic">“And he goes through the sea of affliction, and smites the waves in the sea, and all the depths of the river dry up; and the pride of Asshur will be cast down, and the staff of Egypt will depart.</hi> Zec 10:12. <hi type="italic">And I make them strong in Jehovah; and they will walk in His name, is the saying of Jehovah.” </hi> The subject in Zec 10:11 is Jehovah. He goes, as once He went in the pillar of cloud as the angel of the Lord in the time of Moses, through the sea of affliction. צרה, which has been interpreted in very different ways, we take as in apposition to ים, though not as a permutative, “through the sea, viz., the affliction” (C. B. Mich., Hengst.); but in this sense, “the sea, which caused distress or confinement,” so that the simple reason why  צרה  is not connected with  ים  in the construct state, but placed in apposition, is that the sea might not be described as a straitened sea, or sea of anxiety. This apposition points to the fact which floated before the prophet’s mind, namely, that the Israelites under Moses were so confined by the Red Sea that they thought they were lost (Exo 14:10.). The objection urged by Koehler against this view - namely, that צרה as a noun is not used in the sense of local strait or confinement - is proved to be unfounded by <reference osisRef="Jonah.2.3">Jon 2:3</reference> and Zep 1:15.
